How swmm5-kw should treat splits and loops

Each run gets a fresh engine instance. Nothing leaves this page.

What you are looking at. Stock SWMM routes kinematic wave and steady flow in one upstream-to-downstream pass, so it refuses a junction with two outlets (ERROR 133) and a network where water can come back around (ERROR 131). swmm5-kw is the same EPA 5.2.4 engine with those two refusals replaced by an allocation rule and a per-step iteration.

When there is nothing to split or loop, swmm5-kw writes the same bytes as stock. The Run tab shows that live: the two .out fingerprints match.

The contract

        
    
          
  1. Off means stock. With both options off (the engine's default) the bytes are stock 5.2.4, ERROR 133 and 131 included.
    2. 
          
  2. On changes nothing it has no business changing. A network with nothing to split or loop gives the same bytes as stock in every mode.
    3. 
          
  3. No order dependence. Shuffling the file's junctions and conduits changes nothing.
    4. 
          
  4. Conservation. An allocation never creates water; a loop's leftover is booked to the receiving node. This holds to rounding on every shipped network. The corpus found one defect: HEAD can hand out up to 1.5e-6 cfs more than arrived when the inflow sits within the bisection tolerance of an outlet's capacity. A fix is proposed in the repository, not applied (Doc tab).
    5. 
          
  5. One engine, one answer. The wasm engine matches a native build of the same source and the same maths library byte for byte.
    6.

Forks in the Road


How swmm5-kw teaches EPA SWMM 5.2.4's kinematic wave and steady flow to split a junction and run a loop, what it proved about itself, and what it still cannot do.


The one-way street


Kinematic wave is the plainest honest way to move water through a sewer model. Each pipe takes what its upstream junction hands it, runs that through Manning's equation and the continuity equation, and passes the result on. No pipe ever asks what is happening below it. That is why it is fast. It is also why it is fussy.


Because every pipe waits on its upstream junction, SWMM has to put the pipes in order before it routes a drop: each pipe after every pipe that feeds it. The ordering is called a topological sort, and toposort.c does it once, before the run. A network with one way out of every junction and no way back sorts cleanly. Mathematicians call that shape a tree. So do sewer designers, for the same reason.


Hand stock SWMM 5.2.4 anything else under KINWAVE or STEADY routing and it stops before it starts. A junction with two outlets gets you this:


ERROR 133: Node J2 has more than one outlet link.


A path that leads back to where it began gets you this:


ERROR 131: the following links form cyclic loops in the drainage system:



Why the rule is there


The rule is not an oversight. The engine knows exactly how much water reaches a junction. What it does not know is how to divide it. Dynamic wave never needs telling: it solves for the water surface at every node at once, and the head difference along each pipe settles the share. Kinematic wave has no head to speak of. It knows depth in a pipe, not level at a junction.


So SWMM gives you a node built for the job, the DIVIDER, with four ways to divide (CUTOFF, OVERFLOW, TABULAR and WEIR), and it makes you pick one and supply its numbers. The old Transport block worked the same way with its flow-divider elements. The position is "you tell me how the water splits, and I will route it." That is a sound engineering position.


It is also a tax. Real systems are full of forks: relief sewers, twin barrels laid forty years apart, a storm drain that parts around a building and meets itself on the other side. Each one has to become a divider, and each divider needs a curve somebody made up. A made-up curve is a guess dressed as data, and it does not get better because it sits in an input file.


In September 2026 Bob asked for a SWMM5 whose kinematic wave and steady flow would run loops and node bifurcations. swmm5-kw is that engine.


What swmm5-kw is


swmm5-kw is EPA SWMM 5.2.4, built from the official v5.2.4 tag, with seven source files changed: one new file, kwmod.c, and small edits to flowrout.c, toposort.c, node.c, swmm5.c, swmm5.h and funcs.h, 622 lines added and 4 removed. It has two switches, set through one new API call, swmm_setKwOptions(split, loop). The split switch picks a rule for dividing a junction's outflow among its outlets. The loop switch lets a directed loop iterate within each routing step. Both start off. With both off the engine is stock 5.2.4, byte for byte, refusals included. Dynamic wave is never touched.


One water level for every outlet


The default split rule is called HEAD, and it borrows the one idea kinematic wave lacks. Imagine water standing in the junction at some level, call it y. Every outlet pipe sees that level at its own entrance, less its own offset above the junction floor. At normal depth, each pipe carries whatever Manning's equation gives for that depth. Add up those flows. Too much water leaving? Lower y. Too little? Raise it. Halve the bracket each time, and after 22 to 31 halvings on average (in the test runs) you have the one level at which the outlets together carry exactly what came in.



There is one trap, and it is an old one. A circular pipe carries more than its full-pipe flow when it runs just short of full. The wetted perimeter shrinks faster than the area near the crown, so Manning's flow climbs past full at 0.82 of the diameter and peaks at 1.076 times full flow at 0.94. Let that curve run free and the total is no longer a steady climb in y, and a bisection can be fooled. So HEAD caps each outlet at its full-flow capacity. Water beyond the sum of the capacities stays in the junction and ponds or floods, which is exactly what SWMM's kinematic wave already does with a single pipe that is full.



The other two rules are simpler. CAPACITY divides in proportion to each outlet's full-flow capacity. AREA divides in proportion to each outlet's flow area at the end of the previous step, falling back to CAPACITY on the first step, when every area is zero. AREA was the first rule Bob asked for, in August 2026. All three compute every outlet of a junction together, once per sweep, so the answer cannot depend on which outlet happens to ask first.


What the numbers say


The first test network, split.inp, is as small as a fork can be: one 3 ft pipe carrying 20 cfs into a junction with two outlets, a 3.0 ft pipe and a 1.5 ft pipe, both 400 ft long on the same slope. Stock 5.2.4 refuses it under kinematic wave with ERROR 133 and runs it under dynamic wave. swmm5-kw runs it under all three rules.



HEAD sends 73.8% of the flow down the big pipe. Dynamic wave sends 71.3%. The gap is not a flaw in the rule. It is the one thing dynamic wave can do that kinematic wave cannot: push a pipe past full. Dynamic wave drives 5.73 cfs through the 1.5 ft pipe, about 9% beyond the 5.25 cfs it can carry flowing full by gravity, because the junction's water surface rises and the pipe runs under pressure. Under kinematic wave, full is full. AREA lands in the same place here, because the small pipe is at its cap either way. CAPACITY sends 86.4% down the big pipe and misses by 15 points. Capacity says what a pipe could carry flowing full, not what it takes when both pipes see the same water level.



Two more networks split and rejoin: diamond.inp, one fork and one merge, and braid.inp, two of each. Every pipe's peak flow under swmm5-kw lands within 1.8% of dynamic wave, and within 4.3% on split.inp. Steady flow with HEAD gives a routing continuity error of 0.000% on split.inp; kinematic wave gives 0.131%, about what stock kinematic wave gives on the plain three-pipe chain at 30 cfs (0.124%).



Water that comes back


A loop breaks the sort itself. Kahn's algorithm, which toposort.c uses, repeatedly takes a junction whose inflows are all accounted for. In a loop, every junction is waiting on another, and the algorithm runs out of candidates with pipes still unsorted. Stock SWMM reports ERROR 131 at that point.


swmm5-kw instead picks one junction and declares its waiting over. It takes the unfinished junction with the fewest unsorted inflows; on a tie, the one with the most inflows already sorted, which is the loop's natural entrance; on a further tie, the smallest ID in alphabetical order. That last rule matters more than it looks. The first version broke ties by position in the input file, and the loop models' continuity changed between 0.122% and 0.125% when the file's lines were shuffled. An engine whose answer depends on line order is not an engine you can trust. After sorting, any pipe that delivers water to a junction already processed is marked as loop-closing.


Then, each routing step, the engine has to route water it has not computed yet. It guesses. Each loop-closing pipe is assumed to deliver what it delivered last step. The engine sweeps the network in order, compares what each loop-closing pipe actually routed with the guess, and if they disagree, puts everything back the way it was at the start of the step and sweeps again with better guesses.



"Puts everything back" is the important part. A kinematic-wave pipe carries its state from one step to the next: flow and area at both ends. A trial sweep changes that state. Sweep again without restoring it and the second trial starts from the first trial's answer, which is how you count water twice. After 60 sweeps, or as soon as the guesses stop changing, the engine books any remaining difference to the receiving junction, so the books balance whether the iteration settled or not. On loopactive.inp, a relief pipe that spills from the bottom of the network back to the top, it took 1.55 sweeps per step on average; 5 of 4320 steps reached the cap, and the largest leftover was 0.0019 cfs.


The pipe that ran backwards


Here is the result that matters most, and it corrects something. In September this engine's write-up compared the flow in that relief pipe, R1, under the two methods: 0.51 cfs under swmm5-kw, 3.34 cfs under dynamic wave, and called both of them recirculation. Claude wrote that comparison. It looked only at the size of the two flows. It never looked at their sign.


The sign is the whole story. Under dynamic wave, R1 runs backwards for the entire storm, from J1 to J3, down to -3.34 cfs. The water at J1 stands higher than the water at J3, so the "relief" pipe becomes a second path downstream, beside the main line. That is what a relief pipe in that position would really do. Kinematic wave cannot run a pipe backwards. A link's direction is fixed by the way it is drawn in the input file. So under swmm5-kw, R1 can only carry water the way it points, from J3 back to J1, and it carries 0.51 cfs spilling over its 3.5 ft offset.



loop.inp shows the same thing harder. There dynamic wave sends 30 cfs through a 2 ft outlet under pressure, and kinematic wave, which caps the pipe at full flow, gets 12 cfs through it and floods the rest. Its routing continuity error is -2.25%. September's pipe-by-pipe accounting put all of that imbalance in the two pipes running exactly at capacity, every junction in balance: a stock kinematic-wave behaviour described below.


The lesson is plain, and it belongs on every result swmm5-kw produces for a loop: a kinematic-wave loop is honest only where the ground fixes the direction of every pipe in it, where nothing would ever run backwards. Where backwater would reverse a pipe, kinematic wave is answering a different question, and no amount of iteration will make it answer yours. Loops are exactly where backwater tends to govern. Treat a kinematic-wave loop as screening, never as design.


Proof that nothing else moved


An engine change is easy to make and hard to trust, so this one was built to be checked by machine. The first promise is that where the extension has no work, it does nothing at all. Not "nearly nothing": the same bytes.


Bob's corpus of SWMM5 models (the 1729-SWMM5-Models-2030 repository) supplied the test. The same 3,759 models swmm5-rust was gated on went through stock 5.2.4 and swmm5-kw, side by side, with the same calling sequence. The 357 models that route KINWAVE or STEADY ran four times through swmm5-kw: extension off, then each split rule with loops on. 352 of them gave a .out file identical to stock byte for byte, and a report identical apart from its three clock lines, in all four runs. The 3,239 dynamic-wave models ran with the extension switched on and were identical to stock in 3,226 cases. Models that share interface files ran one at a time, so two runs never wrote the same file: 159 of 163 identical. Not one model differed. 10 more are decks from the OpenSWMM 2026 code review that crash stock 5.2.4 outright; swmm5-kw crashes at the same point and leaves the same partial output, which says the extension changed nothing there and says nothing else, because what C does after a crash like that is undefined. 11 could not be compared at all, because stock 5.2.4 itself never finished.


And how many of those models did the extension actually change? 1: NCIMM_ROUTING/water.inp, which stock refuses with ERROR 131 and swmm5-kw runs. The corpus is a strong test that the extension leaves everything else alone and a weak test of the extension itself, because real models that need it have been converted to dividers or to dynamic wave long ago. The five small networks above are, so far, most of the evidence about the splits themselves.


So the corpus was asked a harder question. Each of its 3,218 dynamic-wave models (all but those that share interface files) was copied with its routing switched to KINWAVE and run through both engines. That is not how anyone built those models, and many fail kinematic wave's other checks first (a regulator that does not leave a storage unit, for one). But it shows how often a real network has a fork or a loop. Stock 5.2.4 refused 925 of them with ERROR 133 or 131. swmm5-kw ran 234 of those to the end. The other 691 stopped on a check the extension leaves alone: a conduit sloping uphill (ERROR 115, in 583 of them), a regulator that does not leave a storage unit (ERROR 139, 357), or a fork with a pump or regulator among its outlets, which keeps stock's ERROR 133 (323). Of the 1,412 that stock could run under kinematic wave, every one gave identical bytes from swmm5-kw; another 874 stopped on an input check in both engines with the same report.


Among the networks swmm5-kw ran, the median had 1 split junction and 0 loop-closing links; the largest had 15 and 8. Their kinematic-wave routing continuity errors had a median magnitude of 0.17%, and 60 of 234 exceeded 1%. That says the extension runs real networks. It says nothing about whether their answers are right: these models were built for dynamic wave, and the backwater they depend on is exactly what kinematic wave leaves out.


The large continuity errors were run down one at a time, with a build that keeps a volume balance for every conduit (tools/conduit_balance.sh). Almost all of those errors are negative, and in SWMM's arithmetic a negative continuity error means the run reports more water leaving than ever came in. Of the 30 largest, 18 make their extra water in conduits pinned at full capacity and 11 in flat conduits that never fill: two stock kinematic-wave behaviours described below. The last is a deck that makes water under stock dynamic wave too (it pumps 5 cfs out of an empty wet well). Three were tested directly by deleting forks until stock 5.2.4 would route the network: XPSWMM/ATTEN.inp, NCIMM_ROUTING/river.inp and XPSWMM/UPWSH1.inp. Each time stock's error was as large as swmm5-kw's or larger. On UPWSH1 stock kinematic wave reports −10,069%: one ditch, full for every step of the run, hands on 39.6 million cubic feet more than it is given.



Three more checks ran on the shipped networks. Shuffling the order of junctions and conduits in the input file changed nothing, in 7 networks with three shuffles each. On those networks no allocation created or destroyed water: the largest difference between what a junction handed out and what it had was 3.6e-15 cfs, which is arithmetic rounding. And the WebAssembly engine this page runs gave the same bytes as a native build of the same source on all 15 runs, provided the native build uses the same maths library. That proviso turned out to be a finding of its own. All three checks share one weakness, which the second outside review found: every shipped junction has two outlets, so none of them could catch a limit that only bites at sixty-five. The section after next tells that story.


The corpus found the one place where that is not true. In XPSWMM/EXTUT17.inp a junction feeds a 1 ft pipe that can carry 0.1126658 cfs and an overflow channel 100 ft up that can carry 14,812. At one step 0.1126642 cfs arrived, a hair under the small pipe's capacity. HEAD's bisection stops when it is within a tolerance set by the junction's total capacity:


if ( fabs(f) <= 1.0e-10 * capSum ) break;


With 14,812 cfs of capacity, that tolerance is 1.48e-6 cfs, coarser than the gap between the inflow and the small pipe's capacity. The bisection stopped just past it, the pipe was marked full at 0.1126658 cfs, and the correction step that follows only adjusts outlets below their caps:


if ( sumFree > 0.0 && qT > sumCapped )


Here the capped pipe alone was over the inflow, so nothing ran, and the junction handed out 1.48e-6 cfs it did not have. It happened in 20 of the 234 corpus networks swmm5-kw routed, never more than 1.48e-06 cfs. At its worst that is a rate of about five fluid ounces an hour. Still a defect: the engine promises never to make water. patch/kw-v1.1-head-overshoot.patch adds one branch, which scales every outlet down to the inflow when the capped ones alone exceed it. On all 234 networks it brings the largest gap to 1.8e-12 cfs and changes output only where the defect fired. It is not applied. Version 1.1 changes the engine for another reason (the next section), so the apps that embed it need the new file anyway; whether this fix rides along is still Bob's decision.


The sixty-fifth outlet


On 31 October Bob passed along a second outside review, of version 1.0. It graded the work 82 out of 100, a B minus. It credited the regression work: 65 runs across the 13 shipped networks, 15 shuffled-order tests and the CAPACITY rule matching the ratio of Manning capacities. Then it listed five ways the engine or this page could mislead. All five reproduced before anything was changed.


The first was in the engine. Build a junction with 65 outlets, every one a 12 in pipe 400 ft long at 1% slope, feed it 20 cfs, and give one outlet a flow limit of 0.1 cfs. Under the AREA rule with steady flow, list the limited outlet first and the junction hands out exactly what arrives. List it 65th and the junction comes up 0.0399 cfs short and floods, with a peak of 0.04 cfs, while the run ends without an error and global continuity still prints 0.000%. Nothing was created; water was held back that should have gone on. The cause was one declaration in the proportional rules:


char done[64];


CAPACITY and AREA divide the water in passes. Each pass shares what is left among the outlets that are not yet full, and an outlet whose share passes its capacity takes the capacity and is marked full. The marks lived in that array, and every use was guarded so it could not overrun:


if ( idx < 64 && done[idx] ) continue;


if ( AllocQ[L] > cap ) { AllocQ[L] = cap; if ( idx < 64 ) done[idx] = 1; capped = 1; }


The guard kept the array safe and made the arithmetic wrong. An outlet past the 64th could be capped but never marked, so the next pass counted it as still open, handed it a share of what was left, and cut it back to its cap again. The share it could not take was lost to the junction. The two-outlet test networks never came near the limit, which is how a correct-looking guard survived every gate.



Version 1.1 keeps the full marks per link, sized when the network is read, so any number of outlets is handled the same way. At 64 outlets or fewer, v1.0 and v1.1 run the same instructions in the same order, and on every shipped network, in six combinations of rule and loop setting, they write identical .out files. A new gate builds the review's junction at 64, 65, 66 and 130 outlets, moves the capped outlet through the boundary positions, and runs all three rules under kinematic wave and steady flow: 78 runs, 0 failures: largest allocation gap 1.2e-13 cfs, no flooding, outlet peaks unchanged by position (largest change 0 cfs). Before the fix the same gate failed 12 of its 78 runs, every AREA run with the capped outlet at position 65 or later.


Did any corpus result depend on the old limit? A census of all 3,759 models counted every node's outgoing links. 1 node in the whole corpus has more than 64: node n in XPSWMM/CTIA_EXI.inp, 65 conduits that each leave it and come straight back, an artefact of a conversion from XPSWMM. That model routes dynamic wave, which the extension never touches, and switched to kinematic wave it stops on an input check before routing a drop. Both versions write identical files for it. So the corpus tables above stand for v1.1 as they are.


The other four findings were in this page, and all four were about trust in what it shows. Run split.inp, pick diamond.inp, and export without running again: the file was named for the diamond and held the split's numbers, because the export took its name from whatever was selected at the moment of the click:


save((CUR.name || 'model').replace(/\.inp$/i, '') + '_swmm5kw_peaks.csv', ...)


Now every run carries a record made when it starts: model, routing, rule, loop setting, time. The export takes its name and a header from that record, and the moment the inputs on the left stop matching it, the results dim and a note says which run they belong to.


Stop swmm5-kw part way through a long run and v1.0 still printed its green headline, "Stock EPA refuses this network; swmm5-kw routes it," because the verdict looked only for error messages, and a stopped run has none. Completion now comes first: a stopped run gets a verdict that says so, with how many reporting periods it wrote out of how many the file asks for, and no comparison table, chart or export is drawn from it.


Peak flows were signed maxima started at minus infinity. A refused run has no series, so its peak was exported as -Infinity; and the relief pipe R1, which dynamic wave runs backwards all storm at down to -3.34 cfs, showed a peak of 0 under dynamic wave, the largest of its values. The essay said so; the live table did not. The table and the export now carry each run's signed maximum, signed minimum and absolute peak, compare runs on the absolute peak, flag any link that runs backwards and in which run, and leave a missing series blank.


The last was the time axis. SWMM writes its first reporting period at the end of the first report step, not at the start, but the chart put sample p at p steps from the left edge, so every curve sat one step early and the last tick could fall outside the chart. The chart now reads each sample's time from the record it came in.



Each of the four page findings has a check in a browser test that drives this page as a person would (12 checks in all). They fail on the v1.0 page and pass on v1.1.


Three things stock 5.2.4 does by itself


Building and checking this engine meant running a great many kinematic-wave models, and three behaviours of unmodified EPA 5.2.4 came to light. None has anything to do with the extension. Each shows up on a network with nothing to split and no loop.


The first is a continuity error at capacity. Feed the chain less than its full-pipe capacity of 33.35 cfs and the routing continuity error is about a tenth of a percent. Feed it a little more and the error grows, steadily, to -10.18% at 37.5 cfs, four cfs over capacity, then drops back to -0.48% at 38 cfs. The minus sign matters: the run reports more water leaving than came in. A model whose peak happens to sit in that band reports a tenth more water out than in. In September only three inflows were run, 30, 34 and 40 cfs, and the worst of the three was -1.60%. The sweep found the band they had stepped over.



The likely cause sits in kinwave.c. When a pipe's inflow reaches full-pipe flow, the solver sets its inlet area to full. Just below, it takes the lower of the two depths that carry that flow, because a circle carries full flow twice, once at 82% depth and once at 100%. A pipe hovering at capacity can flip between the two from one step to the next, a jump of about 18% of the full area, and every flip is booked as stored water that was never there. The sudden recovery at 38 cfs is not explained yet.


The second is that kinematic-wave answers depend on the maths library. The same source compiled against glibc and against musl agree for the first 241 minutes of a storm on the 30 cfs chain and then part company by up to 2% on the recession. Dynamic wave and steady flow gave identical answers under both libraries. So "the same engine" means little for kinematic wave unless you also say which libm it was linked against. The browser engine uses musl's mathematics, and its gate compares against a musl build for exactly that reason.


The third came out of the corpus. Kinematic wave makes water in flat channels, and makes relatively more the less water there is. Run one 1,000 ft trapezoidal channel with no fall at all and a steady 0.03 cfs for a day, and stock 5.2.4 reports a routing continuity error of -11.01%: eleven percent more water out than in. EPA flags such a channel with WARNING 04 and gives it a minimum fall, but the error stays. Give the channel a tenth of a foot of fall and the error is -2.48%; a full foot, -1.21%; at 3 cfs on a foot of fall, -0.22%. Old models converted from other programs are full of flat channels, which is why this showed up in the what-if pass. Where in kinwave.c the extra water comes from has not been traced.



What this does not show


  • That kinematic wave can represent backwater, surcharge or flow reversal. It cannot, in a split or a loop or anywhere else. HEAD is an allocation at normal depth.
  • That swmm5-kw's loop results are fit for design. Where a pipe in a loop would run backwards, the answer is wrong in direction, not just in size.
  • How the three split rules compare across real networks. Five small test networks were compared with dynamic wave. The corpus contains one model the extension changes.
  • Anything about dynamic wave, which the extension never touches.
  • That every continuity error in the what-if pass is stock behaviour. The 30 largest were traced; three of them by a direct test, the rest by a matching signature. The long tail below them was not examined.
  • That the HEAD overshoot fix is right for every network. It was checked on the networks the corpus routes and the shipped ones, and it is not applied.
  • A Windows build. The engine was built and gated on Linux (GCC 13, musl 1.2.4) and as WebAssembly (Clang 18, wasi-libc). EPA's optional .def export file does not list the two new functions.
  • That the corpus was rerun through v1.1. It was not; the outlet census above is the argument that it would give the same bytes.
  • A full visual pass of this page in every browser. The browser checks drive headless Chromium.
  • A person's review of the C changes, line by line. The checks above are mechanical.


How to use it


In this page. Pick a test network or drop in your own .inp, choose a rule, and press Run. The page runs stock EPA 5.2.4, swmm5-kw and a dynamic-wave reference, and shows whether stock refused the model, how each split junction shared its water, and every link's peak flow side by side. The Verify tab runs the gates in your browser.


On your own machine. tools/build.sh builds the extended engine as kwswmm, and stock 5.2.4 beside it. Run KWSPLIT=1 KWLOOP=1 build/kw/kwswmm model.inp model.rpt model.out. KWSPLIT takes 1 for HEAD, 2 for CAPACITY, 3 for AREA; unset means stock. EPA's own CMake build also works on this tree and gives runswmm and libswmm5, which behave as stock until a program calls swmm_setKwOptions.


In another app. wasm/swmm524kw.wasm with wasm/kwengine.js and wasm/wasi-shim.iife.js runs anywhere a browser or Node runs, with no compiler. For a SWMM5 tree of your own, apply patch/swmm524-kw.patch, then run the gates before calling it the same engine.


AI use


This engine, its tests, this page and this essay were made with Claude, Anthropic's AI model, under the direction of Robert (Bob) Dickinson, who asked for kinematic wave and steady flow that run loops and bifurcations, asked for the AREA rule first, chose to keep the work in its own repository, and supplies the model corpus. The engine was written on 29 September 2026; the repository, the corpus gate, this page and the essay on 29 October 2026, with Claude Opus 5.5. Claude designed and wrote the C changes, the test networks, the drivers, the gates, the WebAssembly builds and the JavaScript that runs them, the figures and this text. The checks are mechanical: byte comparison against stock 5.2.4 built from EPA's tag, on the shipped networks and the corpus, and the wasm against native builds. Claude also made the September errors this essay corrects, about the relief pipe and the continuity sweep. On 31 October, for version 1.1, Claude reproduced the five faults in the second outside review Bob supplied, fixed the allocator and the page, and wrote the fan-out gate, the outlet census, the browser checks and the section on them; the 64-slot array it fixed was its own September code. No person has yet reviewed the C changes line by line.

  







  

    

      

        
About swmm5-kw

        
swmm5-kw is EPA SWMM 5.2.4 with one change in purpose: kinematic wave and steady flow routing no longer stop at a junction with several outlets (ERROR 133) or at a directed loop (ERROR 131). A split junction shares its outflow among its outlets by one of three rules; a loop is iterated within each routing step until the flow coming back around settles. Dynamic wave is untouched, and with both options off the engine is stock 5.2.4.

        
This page runs two engines compiled to WebAssembly from the same source tree: stock EPA SWMM 5.2.4 from the official v5.2.4 tag, and the same tree with the extension. The source, the patch, the test networks, the gates and their logs are in the repository SWMMBobSWMM6/swmm5-kw, with the Doc essay as a Word file (dist/swmm5-kw-doc.docx).

        
The EPA Storm Water Management Model is a work of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, in the public domain. Version 5.2.4's engine is Lewis Rossman's design.

        
A modified engine. Results from swmm5-kw with either option on are not stock EPA SWMM results. Its report says so in a KW/SF extension block; keep that block with any result you pass on.

      

      

        
What changed in 1.1

        
A second outside review of v1.0 (31 October 2026) found five faults. Each was reproduced first, then fixed, and each now has a check that fails on v1.0:

        
    
          
  1. Engine. CAPACITY and AREA kept their "outlet is full" marks in char done[64], so at a junction with more than 64 outlets a capped outlet listed 65th or later was never marked: the junction came up short and flooded (0.04 cfs in the review's case). The marks are now per link. A new fan-out gate runs 64, 65, 66 and 130 outlets; no corpus result changes (the one corpus node with 65 outlets is in a model the extension never routes).
    2. 
          
  2. Stale exports. Exporting after picking another model named the file after the new model while it held the old run's numbers. Every run now keeps its own record; results dim when the inputs change, and the export uses the run's name and states its settings.
    3. 
          
  3. Stopped runs. A stopped swmm5-kw run still got the green "routes it" headline. A run that did not finish now gets a "Stopped" verdict saying how far it got, and no comparison or export.
    4. 
          
  4. Peaks. Refused runs exported -Infinity, and a pipe that only ran backwards showed a peak of 0. The table and CSV now give the signed maximum, the signed minimum and the absolute peak, flag reversals, and leave missing values blank.
    5. 
          
  5. Time axis. Samples were drawn one report step early and the last tick could fall outside the chart. Each sample is now drawn at the time stored with it.
    6.

AI use

        
The extension, this page, its tests and the Doc essay were made with Claude, Anthropic's AI model, under the direction of Robert (Bob) Dickinson: the engine in a session on 28 and 29 September 2026, the repository, this page and the essay on 29 October 2026 (Claude Opus 5.5). Bob asked for KW and steady flow that run loops and bifurcations, chose to keep the work in its own repository, and supplies the model corpus it was tested on. Responsibility for publishing the work is his.

        
What Claude did: designed and wrote the allocator (kwmod.c) and the changes to flowrout.c, toposort.c, node.c and swmm5.c; wrote the test networks, the drivers and the gates; built both WebAssembly engines and the JavaScript that runs them; rebuilt everything from EPA's tag in a fresh workspace for this repository; ran the corpus gate; wrote this page, its figures and the essay. On 31 October 2026, for v1.1, it reproduced the five faults in the second outside review Bob supplied, fixed the allocator (its own September code) and this page, and added the fan-out gate, the corpus outlet census and the browser checks.

        
How it was checked: mechanically. Byte comparison of .out and .rpt files against stock 5.2.4 built from the official tag, on the shipped networks and on Bob's corpus; the wasm engines against native builds; the patch against a fresh checkout; this page driven in headless Chromium for the v1.1 checks. The corpus was not rerun through v1.1; a census shows no corpus junction where v1.0 and v1.1 can differ. Not yet checked by a person: the C changes have not been reviewed line by line by Bob, and the split rules have been compared with dynamic wave on five small test networks only.

Kinematic wave, now with forks in the road

    
Stock SWMM's kinematic wave and steady flow need a tree: one way out of every junction, no way back. swmm5-kw lets the water fork and come round again, and leaves everything else byte for byte as EPA wrote it.

    
    
      
  1. Run a test network or your own .inp through stock EPA, swmm5-kw and a dynamic-wave reference, and compare the splits.
    2.
